research.claim: Light sent through two slits one photon at a time arrives as single dots, yet many arrivals build up interference stripes, so light behaves both as a particle and as a wave: wave–particle duality. The probability of landing at a point is the squared size of an amplitude summed over both slits; where the two contributions are out of step they cancel and almost no photons land, even where some land with one slit open. Closing a slit, or detecting which slit each photon used, removes the stripes. Electrons, atoms and molecules do the same.
research.explanation: Late in the 17th century Isaac Newton argued that light is a stream of tiny particles (corpuscles), a view he set out in Opticks in 1704, while Christiaan Huygens described it as a wave. In 1801 Thomas Young described interference of light, and in 1803 he demonstrated it with sunlight, pinholes and cards; these demonstrations, forerunners of the modern two-slit experiment, played a major role in the acceptance of the wave theory. In 1905 Albert Einstein proposed that light itself comes in lumps of energy, later named photons (Gilbert Lewis, 1926). The two pictures meet in the double-slit experiment done with very dim light: G. I. Taylor first saw interference fringes in very dim light in 1909, lowering the light until photon arrivals were mostly separate. Each photon is detected as one dot at one place, and where any one lands is random. With one slit open, many arrivals build a single broad patch. With both open, the arrivals build bands of many hits separated by bands with almost none. Quantum mechanics describes each photon with a wave of probability amplitude that passes through both slits; the two parts overlap, and the chance of detection at each point is the squared size of their sum, high where they arrive in step (crest on crest) and near zero where they arrive half a wavelength out of step (crest on trough). Because amplitudes add before squaring, opening the second slit lowers the count at the dark bands below the one-slit count. Covering a slit leaves one contribution, so nothing cancels and the stripes vanish; so does any measurement that records which slit each photon used. Matter behaves the same way: electron waves were confirmed in 1927 (Davisson and Germer, and Thomson); Claus Jönsson did a two-slit experiment with electrons in 1961; Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi showed single electrons building up the pattern in 1974 (with an electron biprism), and Frabboni and colleagues showed the single-electron build-up through two slits in 2012. The effect has since been seen with atoms, C60 molecules and, in 2019, molecules of about 2,000 atoms.
assumptions: An idealised two-slit setup with a broad single-slit envelope and two equal slits; the picture’s pattern is the envelope times 1 + a² + 2a cos(phase).
Each dot is a pseudo-random sample from the predicted probability pattern, not a simulated path.
No which-path detector is present, except where the narration says a slit is covered.
The light is dim enough that photons arrive one at a time, as in Taylor’s 1909 experiment and later single-photon experiments.
research.prediction: With both slits open, thousands of single arrivals form stripes whose dark bands receive fewer hits than the same spots receive with one slit open; with one slit closed, the arrivals form a single patch.
research.falsifier: If single-particle arrivals with both slits open simply added up the two one-slit patterns, with no dark bands below the one-slit level, the wave description would be wrong.
limitations: The waves drawn depict the probability amplitude, not a path; the picture never shows which slit a particle used.
The one-slit patch is drawn centred between the slits, as it would be with parallel light and a distant screen; with a lamp this close it would sit higher, in line with the open slit.
Particle wavelengths, detector efficiency and decoherence are not modelled.
misconceptions: Each photon splits in two: it is always detected whole, in one place.
The stripes come from photons bumping into each other: they appear even when only one photon is in the apparatus at a time.
Light is either a particle or a wave: neither picture alone explains the experiment.

Does each photon split in two?
What happens if you detect which slit was used?

scene.title: Wave–particle duality: the double-slit experiment
scene.subtitle: Send light through two slits, one photon at a time. Each lands as a single dot, yet thousands of dots build up stripes. Is light a particle or a wave?
scene.why: For centuries, people argued over whether light is made of particles or waves. Send it through two slits one photon at a time, and it behaves like both.
scene.opening: Is light made of tiny particles, or is it a wave?

beats.title: Particles of light
beats.body: Imagine a laser so dim its light lands on a screen one dot at a time. Each dot is a photon, one tiny lump of light that got through the slit. Isaac Newton thought light was just that: a spray of tiny particles.

beats.title: One slit, thousands of dots
beats.body: Now let thousands of photons through. With one slit open, they pile up in one soft patch. Just what a spray of tiny particles would do.

beats.title: Open the second slit
beats.body: Now slide the cover off the second slit. Something faint spreads from both slits, yet each lands as one dot. At first, the dots look scattered at random.

beats.title: Stripes appear
beats.body: After thousands more dots, stripes appear. Between the stripes are gaps where almost none land. One slit alone sends dots there, but opening the second takes them away.

beats.title: Light acts like a wave
beats.body: In 1803, Thomas Young saw such stripes in sunlight: light acts like a wave. Like two pebbles in a pond, both slits send out ripples that cross. Where two tops meet, dots pile up; where a top meets a dip, the ripples cancel.

beats.title: Both at once
beats.body: Cover one slit and start again: with one set of ripples, no stripes form. So light travels like a wave, yet lands like a particle. This is wave–particle duality, and electrons and atoms show it too.

beats.title: Watching the slits
beats.body: Open both slits, and imagine a sensor at one that clicks as a photon passes. Clicked photons, in purple, took that slit; the rest took the other. Once the path is known, the two ripples can no longer add and cancel.

beats.title: Why watching matters
beats.body: A record of the path is enough; the sensor needn't push the photon. The record marks one slit's ripples, purple here, so they can't cancel. Why each photon lands at just one spot is still debated today.

scene.takeaway: Light travels like a wave, through both slits at once, but always lands as a single dot, like a particle. Learn which slit it took, and the stripes vanish.

questions.q: So is light a wave or a particle?
questions.a: Both, in a sense: it travels as a wave that passes through both slits, and it is detected as single photons, one dot at a time. Neither picture alone explains the experiment.

questions.q: Can you really put a sensor on a slit?
questions.a: For light, a sensor that caught the photon would stop it, so this is a thought experiment. A simple real version puts a polarizing filter, like the lens of polarized sunglasses, over each slit: one passes light that shakes up and down, the other side to side. Light shaking in different directions can't cancel, so the stripes vanish, though the filters don't push the photons aside.

questions.q: Does someone have to look at the sensor?
questions.a: No. The stripes vanish whenever the path is recorded, even if nobody reads it. The dots then land as the two slits' single-slit patterns added together.

questions.q: Is it still a mystery?
questions.a: Partly. Why the stripes vanish is well understood: once the two paths can be told apart, their waves no longer add and cancel, and the clearer the record, the fainter the stripes. Why each photon lands at one definite spot is the measurement problem, and it is still debated.

questions.q: Does each photon split in two?
questions.a: No. Each one is always found as one whole dot on the screen. What passes through both slits is the wave that sets where it may land.

questions.q: Why do the dots look random at first?
questions.a: Each landing spot is a matter of chance. Only the odds are fixed, and the odds show up once thousands of dots have landed.

questions.q: Has this really been done one photon at a time?
questions.a: Yes. G. I. Taylor first saw stripes like these in very dim light in 1909, and single-particle interference has since been seen with single photons, electrons, atoms and molecules of about 2,000 atoms.

On 2026-11-19, at the owner’s request, it was redrawn in a coding session in perspective after a reference the owner gave (a lamp, a barrier with two upright slits and a screen), and a last chapter adds a sensor at one slit: once the path is known, the stripes give way to one soft patch. scene.title: The double-slit experiment: how can single particles make stripes?
scene.subtitle: Fire particles one at a time at a wall with two slits. Each lands as a single dot, yet thousands of dots build up stripes, because each particle passes through the slits as a wave.
scene.why: Electrons, atoms and molecules fired one at a time still build up stripes. Each lands as a dot, but before it lands it spreads like a wave through both slits.
scene.opening: If particles go through the slits one by one, where do the stripes come from?

beats.title: One at a time
beats.body: Imagine a gun that fires tiny particles, one at a time. Each goes through a slit in a wall and hits a screen. It lands as a single dot.

beats.title: Thousands of dots
beats.body: Keep firing, thousands of times. With one slit open, they pile up in one soft patch. The bars on the right count where they land.

beats.title: Open the second slit
beats.body: Now slide the cover off the second slit. Again, each particle lands as one dot. At first, the dots look scattered at random.

beats.title: Stripes appear
beats.body: After thousands more dots, stripes appear. Between the stripes are gaps where almost none land. One slit alone sent dots there; the second slit took them away.

beats.title: A wave through both slits
beats.body: On its way, each particle acts like a spreading wave. The wave goes through both slits and takes two paths to each spot. Where crest meets crest, dots pile up; crest on trough, none land.

beats.title: Close a slit
beats.body: Now cover the second slit, clear the screen and fire again. With one way through, there is nothing to cancel: no stripes. Electrons, atoms and even big molecules all behave this way.

scene.takeaway: Each particle lands as one dot, but where it can land is set by a wave that passes through both slits. Where the two parts of the wave cancel, no particle lands, so stripes build up.

questions.q: Does each particle split in two?
questions.a: No. Each one is always found as one whole dot on the screen. What spreads through both slits is the wave that sets where it may land.

questions.q: Why do the dots look random at first?
questions.a: Each landing spot is a matter of chance. Only the odds are fixed, and the odds show up once thousands of dots have landed.

questions.q: Why does opening a second slit leave some spots empty?
questions.a: There the wave from one slit arrives out of step with the wave from the other, and they cancel, so the chance of landing there drops to almost zero.

questions.q: What if you watch which slit each particle goes through?
questions.a: Then the stripes disappear and the dots pile up as if from two single slits. Knowing the path removes the overlap of the two waves.

questions.q: Has this really been done one particle at a time?
questions.a: Yes. Electrons were shown building up stripes one by one in 1974 and again in 2012, and molecules of up to 2,000 atoms have shown stripes too.

scene.title: Wave–particle duality: the double-slit experiment
scene.subtitle: Send light through two slits, one photon at a time. Each lands as a single dot, yet thousands of dots build up stripes. Is light a particle or a wave?
scene.why: For centuries, people argued over whether light is made of particles or waves. Send it through two slits one photon at a time, and it behaves like both.
scene.opening: Is light made of tiny particles, or is it a wave?

beats.title: Particles of light
beats.body: Imagine a laser so dim its light lands on a screen one dot at a time. Each dot is a photon, one tiny lump of light that got through the slit. Isaac Newton thought light was just that: a spray of tiny particles.

beats.title: One slit, thousands of dots
beats.body: Now let thousands of photons through. With one slit open, they pile up in one soft patch. Just what a spray of tiny particles would do.

beats.title: Open the second slit
beats.body: Now slide the cover off the second slit. Something faint spreads from both slits, yet each lands as one dot. At first, the dots look scattered at random.

beats.title: Stripes appear
beats.body: After thousands more dots, stripes appear. Between the stripes are gaps where almost none land. One slit alone sends dots there, but opening the second takes them away.

beats.title: Light acts like a wave
beats.body: In 1803, Thomas Young saw such stripes in sunlight: light acts like a wave. Like two pebbles in a pond, both slits send out ripples that cross. Where two tops meet, dots pile up; where a top meets a dip, the ripples cancel.

beats.title: Both at once
beats.body: Cover one slit and start again: with one set of ripples, no stripes form. So light travels like a wave, yet lands like a particle. This is wave–particle duality, and electrons and atoms show it too.

beats.title: Watching the slits
beats.body: Open both slits, and imagine a sensor at one that clicks as a photon passes. Clicked photons, in purple, took that slit; the rest took the other. Once the path is known, the two ripples can no longer add and cancel.

beats.title: Why watching matters
beats.body: A record of the path is enough; the sensor needn't push the photon. The record marks one slit's ripples, purple here, so they can't cancel. Why each photon lands at just one spot is still debated today.

scene.takeaway: Light travels like a wave, through both slits at once, but always lands as a single dot, like a particle. Learn which slit it took, and the stripes vanish.

questions.q: So is light a wave or a particle?
questions.a: Both, in a sense: it travels as a wave that passes through both slits, and it is detected as single photons, one dot at a time. Neither picture alone explains the experiment.

questions.q: Can you really put a sensor on a slit?
questions.a: For light, a sensor that caught the photon would stop it, so this is a thought experiment. A simple real version puts a polarizing filter, like the lens of polarized sunglasses, over each slit: one passes light that shakes up and down, the other side to side. Light shaking in different directions can't cancel, so the stripes vanish, though the filters don't push the photons aside.

questions.q: Does someone have to look at the sensor?
questions.a: No. The stripes vanish whenever the path is recorded, even if nobody reads it. The dots then land as the two slits' single-slit patterns added together.

questions.q: Is it still a mystery?
questions.a: Partly. Why the stripes vanish is well understood: once the two paths can be told apart, their waves no longer add and cancel, and the clearer the record, the fainter the stripes. Why each photon lands at one definite spot is the measurement problem, and it is still debated.

questions.q: Does each photon split in two?
questions.a: No. Each one is always found as one whole dot on the screen. What passes through both slits is the wave that sets where it may land.

questions.q: Why do the dots look random at first?
questions.a: Each landing spot is a matter of chance. Only the odds are fixed, and the odds show up once thousands of dots have landed.

questions.q: Has this really been done one photon at a time?
questions.a: Yes. G. I. Taylor first saw stripes like these in very dim light in 1909, and single-particle interference has since been seen with single photons, electrons, atoms and molecules of about 2,000 atoms.

Flat wavefronts suit a collimated laser. All model and render checks pass; the history is unchanged and right.
